skyline.text: Amit Varma on why a statute needs a state behind it
How kept-alive firms cost Japan thirty years, by Ajay Shah
The bankruptcy code promised in 2013 that never made it in

footnote.text: The loss has already taken place.

brief.head: Medium foolish
brief.text: Promoters who siphon off cash can do it a couple of times, Ajay Shah said, before lenders wise up. India’s credit markets are “medium foolish”, not deeply foolish. {080-J06}

brief.head: A suspect word
brief.text: “The word stakeholder is a sure sign of feeble reasoning,” Ajay Shah said. Whether to sell or break up a failed firm is a cold business call. {080-C04}

brief.head: Banks prefer the dark
brief.text: Banks, Ajay Shah said, like to negotiate in darkness, one creditor at a time, rather than before the full committee. Amit Varma’s reply: sunlight is the best disinfectant. {080-J18}

brief.head: A virtuous cycle
brief.text: India’s reforms of 1991 to 2011 worked, Ajay Shah said, because capital controls, the equity market, software and telecom were being fixed in parallel, each strengthening the others. {080-C15}

brief.head: First things first
brief.text: Ajay Shah and Vijay Kelkar zero-base the state: foreign policy, the military, fiat money, police and courts, taxes and commercial law come before causes like health. {080-C16}

thought.text: To take interest in firms is to take interest in birth and death.
thought.who: Ajay Shah, explaining why an episode about firms must also be about their death

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on how firms should die
lead.head: Let dead firms lie
body: Amit Varma began by declaring that firms are awesome, amazing, edifying and illuminating. Ajay Shah had come to talk about how they die.
The economist Joseph Schumpeter’s creative destruction, Shah said, needs both birth and death: “You need the creation of firms, you need Vishnu, and you need Shiv.” {080-C01}
When an old firm fails, he said, its labour and capital are not lost. They flow back to other firms, as a body’s atoms return to other forms of life.
What followed was Shah’s masterclass on how bankruptcy should work, and how it has worked in India, where he sat on the committee that shaped the law.
## The day of default
A company, Shah said, is run by its shareholders only while they pay their dues. The day they default, they are thrown out, and the creditors take control. {080-C03}
A judge has two questions to settle, and only two: was there credit, and was there a default?
After that, speed is everything. A failing firm is “a melting ice cube”, Shah said: key employees leave, suppliers hold back goods, machines go unmaintained. {080-C06}
Delay has another cost. A firm propped up with fresh loans becomes a zombie, eating the margins of healthy rivals. Japan, Shah said, lost thirty years this way.
Once in charge, creditors must decide whether the firm is worth more kept running or broken up. That, Shah insisted, is a business judgment, not a humanitarian one.
Their forum is the committee of creditors, where clashing claims are haggled over. What India needs, he said, is “a badass commercially sophisticated committee of creditors”. {080-C08}
## A C-grade code
India’s Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code became law in 2016. Shah’s verdict on the reform he helped bring about was blunt: “it is a B grade or a C grade project so far.”
Varma protested that the work of Shah, Susan Thomas and Bhargavi Zaveri-Shah was being dismissed “by some random uncle as third rate”.
The trouble starts with the banks. Their overriding objective, Shah said, is “how to hide the bad news”: they delay, and worry more about a future CBI investigation than about recovering money.

The NCLT works like any other Indian court. The new regulator was built from eight sections pasted out of the SEBI Act. And promoters, barred from bidding for their own firms, quietly restructure loans with banks in secret.
## In the shadow of the law
The real test, Shah argued, is the outcome: a credit market where borrowers are keen to repay and lenders keen to lend.
Few cases should need a court. “In advanced economies, most transactions are privately negotiated between the creditors and the shareholders under the threat of the law,” he said. {080-C12}

Varma called “in the shadow of the law” the key phrase of the episode. The law, he argued, is more than a statute: it includes state capability and the expectation of enforcement. “Unless all of that is in place, just writing a great law doesn’t make sense.”

Above all, Shah said, a reform needs researchers and critics to keep it honest. India produces perhaps two papers a year on bankruptcy where twenty are needed. Without that pipeline, “nothing will ever get fixed”.

second.label: The regulator
second.head: Cut, paste, malfunction
second.deck: How 140 sections for a new regulator gave way to eight from SEBI
body: The original draft of India’s bankruptcy law had about 140 sections on how to build its new regulator, the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India: checks and balances, separation of powers, governance, Ajay Shah said. {080-S05}
All of it was deleted. Instead, someone cut and pasted some eight sections from the SEBI Act into the IBBI, and SEBI’s malfunctions came with them.

The IBBI then hit the limits of Indian state capability on day one, along with the pull every government agency feels towards more power. In a British common law system, Shah added, such rules would evolve as market practice. India waits for the regulator to write them. {080-C11}

quote.text: So all the bad practices of how SEBI malfunctions were brought into IBBI.

second.caption: the regulator that was cut and pasted

third.head: A rat trap under the chair
body: In India, the promoter of a bankrupt firm cannot even bid to buy it back. In principle, Ajay Shah said, that is a mistake: promoters know the business best and would probably bid higher.

But he accepts the counter-argument. A promoter expecting to return could leave poison pills: “messy things inside the company that she knows about, that she understands, that she will be able to defuse once she is back in charge”. {080-C10}
Amit Varma pictured “a rat trap in the corner office under the chair under the table”. “That’s literally what can be done,” Shah replied. {080-J09}
With weak rule of law, he said, such traps go unpunished. So India has two bad extremes: promoters shut out of formal bankruptcy, and banks quietly restructuring their loans in secret.
third.caption: poison pills

p2.title: Last rites
p2.deck: Ajay Shah’s masterclass on how bankruptcy should work, and why India’s code falls short

sections.label: First principles
sections.head: Vishnu builds, Shiva clears
sections.caption: creative destruction
body: Creative destruction, Ajay Shah said, needs birth and death alike: Vishnu and Shiva. Without both, he said, “the harmony of the world is incomplete.” {080-C01}

Firms take labour and capital and organise them in particular ways, he said, much as an organism’s DNA holds the recipe for assembling atoms and molecules. It is easy to grow emotional about either. But the recipe may be a bad one, or the world may move on.

In the economist Joseph Schumpeter’s story of progress, innovators take risks and earn a temporary monopoly on a new idea, and the prospect of that rent drives research. Old firms that cannot keep up go bankrupt, and their labour and capital pass to other firms.
## Adapt or make way

Amit Varma offered two axioms: the world is complex, and the world is in flux. {080-C02} So people’s needs cannot be met by central planning, only from the bottom up, through the price system Friedrich Hayek described.

Firms that meet needs earn profits. Adaptation, Varma said, “is learning how to keep serving other people in society”, and a firm that fails to adapt should go out of business so its labour and resources can be better used.
~ Some firms do adapt. The Tata Steel of 2024, Shah said, is unrecognisably different from Jamsetji Tata’s. Many others will not manage it, and should go out of business. {080-J14}

quote.text: One of them is that the world is complex, and the other one is that the world is in flux.

sections.label: The firm
sections.head: When creditors take the keys
sections.caption: what happens on default
body: A firm starts with capital from its shareholders and usually borrows too, Ajay Shah said. Borrowing need not mean a bank loan: rent camera equipment for a show and pay later, and the owner is your creditor. Operational and financial creditors are both creditors.

As the company was conceived in Europe in the 15th and 16th centuries, the shareholders make every decision as long as they service their debts. The creditor has no say, only a claim: pay in 100 rupees, expect 110 after a year. {#interest}
## A new balance sheet
When the firm fails to pay, a creditor goes before a judge, who need establish only that there was credit and a default. Then the shareholders lose control and, usually, their capital too. {080-C03}

Take a company with 100 rupees of equity and 100 of debt that defaults. It is rebuilt on a brand new balance sheet, with the equity holders gone and the creditors in control. “It is that deep,” Shah said.

~ Too many Indians, he lamented, miss these basics and grow sentimental about a company, its old shareholders and its founding family. In 15th- and 16th-century England, he said, there was no sentimentalism around such things.

quote.text: The day the shareholders fail to pay their dues, they’re supposed to get thrown out and replaced by the creditors.

sections.label: The case for speed
sections.head: Propped up, dragging down
sections.caption: zombie firms and melting ice cubes
body: Suppose a weak firm is propped up with more and more debt, Ajay Shah said, because badly regulated banks will not admit the problem or the government is prodding them. It keeps competing with healthy firms and damaging their profit margins.
“These firms that are dead men walking are called zombie firms,” he said. Banks in the same state are zombie banks. {080-C05}
Without profits, healthy firms do not invest. A kept-alive Air India or Jet Airways, Shah said, drives down fares and harms quality airlines like Vistara. {#vistara}
## The ice cube
Delay also helps the guilty. A promoter family always knows more than outsiders, Shah said, and when it sees trouble coming it may start stealing cash. Every week of delay gives it more time.
Meanwhile the firm falls apart: key employees leave, suppliers hold back goods, maintenance is skipped. “Once a firm starts getting into trouble, it’s a melting ice cube,” he said. {080-C06}
~ What every healthy society needs, Shah argued, is an objective early warning that sets the bankruptcy process going fast. Business failure is normal, he said, and should carry no stigma. {#stigma}

quote.text: Japan went through thirty years of misery because they had zombie banks which were keeping zombie firms aloft.

sections.label: The bargaining table
sections.head: Haggling, with a supermajority
sections.caption: the committee of creditors
body: Caught early, a failing firm is worth more as a going concern than broken up, Ajay Shah said. Its people, processes, IT systems, culture and outside relationships add up to intangible capital, often worth a lot. Caught late, only liquidation is left. {080-C07}
Choosing between them is a business judgment, not a humanitarian one, Shah said; his example set 40 from liquidation against 70 from a sale as a going concern. {#forty}
## Who holds the factory

Creditors’ interests clash. A secured lender holding the key factory can threaten to torpedo a going-concern plan unless it is paid first: “I want my hundred and you guys figure out whatever else you want to do.”
Decisions need a supermajority, not just 51 per cent but perhaps 60 or 70. {#supermajority}
Doing this well takes sophisticated bargaining, Shah said, which rarely happens in India because most financial firms are “regulated to death” and run as bureaucracies. {080-C08}

~ Many good bids are not all cash but promises to repay over years. Judging whether to trust the bidder cannot be reduced to opening bids like government procurement, though that, Shah said, has been India’s instinct.

quote.text: If you get there soon enough, actually the value of the firm as a going concern is higher than the sum of the parts.

sections.label: The real world
sections.head: Hiding the bad news
sections.caption: why banks drag their feet
body: India has a bankruptcy process now, and it is better to have it than not, Ajay Shah said. But it is not a great one. {#cgrade}

The first problem is the banks. By the time of bankruptcy, Shah said, the loss has already happened; the only question is who bears it. Yet banks carry the loan at full value and want to delay recognising the loss. {080-C09}
Amit Varma described evergreening: the bank lends the borrower fresh money to repay the old loan, and the can is kicked down the road.
## Painting the tape

Put such banks on a committee of creditors and they will propose another meeting next month, Shah said, while the firm melts. Public sector and private bankers alike think of the CBI, and of whether a future investigation will find fault. {#cbi}

“That’s different from a commercial instinct,” he said. His unorthodox fix, which he admitted would be hard to sell: until banking regulation gets its act together, cut the voting power of banks in the committee, since mutual funds, foreign investors, NBFCs and insurers are more commercial.

~ Varma worried that bankers would not know the first thing about a bankrupt biscuit factory. Shah disagreed: they lent it a hundred crore rupees, so “they’re bloody well going to understand your industry”. {080-J07}

quote.text: So a core insight in bankruptcy is a business has failed, the loss has already taken place.

sections.label: The way forward
sections.head: Living in the law’s shadow
sections.caption: the shadow of the law
body: Public policy, Ajay Shah said, can be judged by its inputs, outputs and outcomes. In bankruptcy, the inputs are the law, the NCLT and the committees; the outputs are cases and the money creditors get back.

The outcome that matters is a working credit market. Leverage in India, he said, should go up when a bankruptcy code comes in, and most disputes should be resolved by private negotiation, “in the shadow of the law”. {080-C12}

For Amit Varma, the law in that phrase is more than a statute on paper. It is the invisible infrastructure of state capability and enforcement, and when that is broken, the damage is “turtles all the way down”. {080-J19}
## Strong law, weak ground

A good law in a vacuum, Varma argued, means nothing. {080-C13} Shah framed it as a trade-off: pass a good law that performs weakly today and improves as other pieces fall into place, or settle for a weaker compromise suited to present conditions.
~ Either way, Shah said, passing the law and inaugurating the regulator is only the beginning. Then starts “a process of iterative refinement”, with data and researchers keeping the reform honest.

quote.text: there is nothing called a good law or a good policy in a vacuum.

side.boxText: The economist Joseph Schumpeter tied progress to the birth and death of firms. Innovators earn a temporary monopoly rent on new ideas; old firms that cannot keep up go bankrupt. Creative destruction, Ajay Shah said, requires both. {080-C01}

contQuote.text: And I think most people in India don’t understand the importance of the knowledge ecosystem. That every area of work has to be ensconced in a successful knowledge ecosystem.

p3.deck: How India got its bankruptcy code, and the zombies it was meant to bury

stories.caption: how a budget paragraph grew into a law
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah retells KP Krishnan’s story of the code
stories.head: The paragraph that grew a code
body: In 2015, part A of the budget speech carried a paragraph from the Ministry of Small and Medium Enterprises, promising a bankruptcy code for small companies. {080-S03}

KP Krishnan took that paragraph to Jaitley, the finance minister, Ajay Shah said, retelling a story Krishnan had told on *The Seen and the Unseen*. They could do that, Krishnan said, but could they not do bigger, with a full bankruptcy code?
Jaitley’s question was practical: “Do we have the ability? Do we have the teams?”

Krishnan pointed to the Financial Sector Legislative Reforms Commission, led by Justice Srikrishna from 2011 to 2015, which had shown that India could run large research teams and draft big, complex laws to a world-class standard. {#fslrc}
So a committee called the BLRC was set up, led by TK Viswanathan, a wise old hand from the world of the law ministry. Shah and Susan Thomas were among its members.

Even then, it began with a narrow plan: a few amendments to the Companies Act’s winding-up provisions. It took a while for people to see that a bankruptcy code plays at a different level, as a negotiation mechanism for creditors.
Rajiv Mehrishi, who became secretary of the Department of Economic Affairs, backed the more radical view: not “dinky trivial refinements” but a full code.
~ Susan Thomas led the team that wrote the first draft, which became law in 2016 as the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code.
stories.why: Big reform needs an ambitious ask and a believable answer to whether it can be done. Here the answer came from capability the FSLRC had built earlier, and even then a narrow vision had to be overcome.
stories.postscript: Amit Varma, who discussed the drafting with Bhargavi Zaveri-Shah of Susan Thomas’s team, calls the inside story “absolutely inspiring”.

stories.caption: the bankruptcy code that never was
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on the Companies Act of 2013
stories.head: The chapters that never came
body: When India was writing its new Companies Act of 2013, Ajay Shah said, Montek Singh Ahluwalia, deputy chairman of the Planning Commission, told the Ministry of Company Affairs it should contain chapters forming a full bankruptcy code, with collective negotiation among creditors. {#chapters}
He was assured it would be done. It was not.
When Shah later raised the issue, Montek asked whether he was sure the code was not in the Act. Shah was. “I have done my fair share of bedtime reading of the Companies Act,” he said. {080-S02}
~ There were some trivial winding-up provisions, he said, but no bankruptcy process. It took a long time for people to understand such basics.
stories.why: A promise made in a ministry is not law on paper. A real bankruptcy code is a negotiation mechanism for creditors, quite unlike winding-up clauses, and it took someone who had actually read the statute to say so.

stories.start: the single great insight of Japan in the bad years after 1986
stories.end: And in fact it cost thirty years of economic dynamism in Japan.
stories.caption: Japan’s zombie banks
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on what zombies cost Japan
stories.head: A thirty-year hangover
body: After 1986, Ajay Shah said, Japan’s Ministry of Finance and MITI ran an industrial policy that kept bad firms artificially alive, propped up by bad banks. {080-S04}

The zombie firms kept competing with healthy ones. “The presence of these zombies shatters profitability for everybody else,” Shah said, so economic dynamism drained away across the country. {#shatters}
The cost, he said, ran to thirty years, and the whole thing went badly wrong. Healthy firms need profits in order to invest, and zombies take those profits away.

~ Amit Varma noted that Japan also made a lot of great zombie movies, and wondered whether to go back and watch them with new eyes, for metaphors beneath the surface: “dead man walking, axe in hand, hand chopped off”. {080-J04}
stories.why: Keeping dead firms alive is not kindness, on Shah’s account. It drains the profits that healthy firms need in order to invest, and as Japan found, the bill can run for decades.

stories.caption: the word that offended a committee
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on a committee that took offence
stories.head: Not rude, just technical
body: Long ago, Ajay Shah said, he sat on the Percy Mistry committee on Bombay as an international financial centre.
There he and Mistry kept using the term “zombie bank”, and some members took offence, thinking it a disrespectful word. {080-S01}
But it is a technical word, Shah said. Zombie firms and zombie banks are terms that came out of the research on Japan, for institutions that are dead men walking.

~ Amit Varma, who had just been musing on Japan’s zombie movies, admitted that his own memory was “pretty close to being a zombie”. {#memory} He thought the very first episode of *The Seen and the Unseen* was on zombie banks, and urged listeners to look it up.

quote.text: And there Percy and I were merrily bandying the word zombie bank around. And some people in the committee got very offended.

quiz.q: Which two gods did Ajay Shah say Schumpeterian creative destruction needs?
quiz.a: Vishnu for the creation of firms, and Shiva for their destruction.

quiz.q: What two questions alone should a judge ask when a creditor alleges default?
quiz.a: Whether there was a credit relationship, and whether there was indeed a default.

quiz.q: How long did Japan suffer from zombie banks keeping zombie firms aloft, by Shah’s account?
quiz.a: Thirty years of misery, in the bad years after 1986.

quiz.q: What replaced the 140 sections drafted to build India’s new bankruptcy regulator, the IBBI?
quiz.a: Some eight sections cut and pasted from the SEBI Act, malfunctions and all.

quiz.q: Why does Shah want to cut the voting power of banks on committees of creditors?
quiz.a: Banks hide losses and fear future CBI probes; other creditors are more commercial.

quiz.q: What is a poison pill in the bankruptcy of a promoter-run firm?
quiz.a: A hidden trap the promoter leaves, which only she knows how to defuse.
